Where it began

Andrew Strauss was born in Johannesburg on 2 March 1977 and came to Britain when he was six. He went to Caldicott School in Buckinghamshire and then Radley College, before reading economics at Durham University.

At Durham he also played rugby at fly-half, climbing from the third XV to the second, until his university cricket coach, Graeme Fowler, talked him into giving his full attention to cricket. The university awarded him a full Palatinate for his cricket. He made his Middlesex debut in 1998 with 83 in his first first-class innings, and by 2002 he was captain of the county.

The player

Strauss announced himself at Lord's in 2004, called up against New Zealand when Michael Vaughan was ruled out. He made 112 in the first innings, was run out short of a second hundred in the second, and took the match award. That winter, back in the country of his birth, he scored 126 and 94 not out in his first Test abroad, and went on to be player of the series.

He made two hundreds in the 2005 Ashes, the only man on either side to do so, and became England captain on a permanent basis in January 2009. That summer he led them to a 2–1 Ashes win, top-scoring for either side with 474 runs, including 161 at Lord's in England's first Ashes Test win there for 75 years. In 100 Tests he made 7,037 runs at 40.91 with 21 hundreds, and as captain in 49 Tests he won 23.

What made him special

He was a back-foot player who loved the cut and the pull, and he was a superb catcher at slip. In 2012 he passed Ian Botham and Colin Cowdrey for the most catches by an England fielder, and finished with 121 before Alastair Cook later went past him. When he retired in 2012, the reporters at his farewell press conference applauded him, a rare thing.

One-day cricket was not always as kind to him as Tests, though he did once make 152 against Bangladesh. And his bowling was a well-kept secret: in Zimbabwe in 2004 he was handed a single over in a one-day game and gave away three runs, which is respectable for a man who spent most of his time at slip.

Away from the middle

He became an MBE after the 2005 Ashes and an OBE in 2011, and was knighted in 2019 for his services to English cricket. Durham gave him an honorary doctorate in 2011. In 2015 he took on the job of Director of Cricket at the ECB. He also served on the MCC committee, and wrote several books, among them Coming Into Play and his autobiography, Driving Ambition. And he became president of the Primary Club Juniors, which raises money for blind cricket.

And finally

For that charity he once took part in a blind cricket match, blindfolded, and was out to his second ball. He also collected an impressive list of nicknames over the years, from Straussy and Levi to The General and, best of all, Mr Potato Head.
